_purpose: An enum you can create must also be an enum you can fill. asset_create already made the asset and reported success, but the engine builds a User Defined Enum with an empty name array, so it arrived with no entries: a variable could be typed to it and a switch on it had no case pins. This walks the whole path - create, add entries, read them back, use it in a graph - and then pins the refusals and the renumbering that remove and move cause.
_reading: The switch assertions are the ones that matter. Case pins are named after the stored NewEnumerator<n>, not the authored name, so 'shown_as' is what tells a caller which pin is theirs. A switch with only execute and Selection is what an unfillable enum used to produce.
_requires: Any project. Creates an enum and a Blueprint under /Game/UplinkScenarios and deletes them again.

steps._note: Housekeeping: clear debris from an aborted earlier run.
A freshly created enum has NO entries. Not one placeholder - none. This is what made the asset useless before there was any way to add to it.
Three entries, and the trailing _MAX the engine adds is not one of them.
REFUSED: a name already in use. Checked before the entry is added, so a refusal leaves no NewEnumerator<n> behind.
REFUSED: renaming onto another entry's name.
REFUSED: index 3 is the hidden _MAX slot. The engine's own bounds check admits it and then inserts past the end of a list that excludes _MAX, so this one is bounded here instead.
The enum is now usable: a variable typed to it, and a switch that actually has cases.
The switch's case pins carry the stored names and report the authored ones as shown_as. Before entries could be added, this node had only execute and Selection.

Addressed by the STORED name rather than the authored one. That is the spelling a Switch node's case pins carry, so a caller who read a pin can act on it here without a translation step - and it is the spelling that does not move when the entry is renamed or the editor runs in another language.
A rename changes only the name it shows under - the value stays put.
A remove does NOT: the engine re-sequences every value to 0..n-1 afterwards, so anything already storing one of those numbers now means a different entry. Reported rather than left to be discovered.
The blueprint that uses it still compiles after the enum changed under it.
